name: Lævateinn
maker: Unnamed (forged with rune magic in some readings)
powers: The only weapon said able to slay the rooster Viðófnir at the top of the world tree.
description: The 'wounding wand' of Fjölsvinnsmál, the blade with which alone the rooster Viðófnir, perched at the top of the world tree, could be slain. It lies in a chest beside the giantess Sinmara, bound by nine locks that only a feather plucked from Viðófnir's own tail can open. Scholars debate whether it is Loki's sword or a separate weapon; its name may itself be a late emendation.

name: Lasabrjótur
powers: Said to open locks, fetters, and binding magic.
description: Lasabrjótur, the lock-breaker of the Huld manuscript, a stave said to open locks and fetters. Its name literally means 'breaker of latches'. It was the kind of sign that made the Icelandic staves feared as well as respected, promising a power over iron and bindings that no ordinary key could match.

name: Lukkustafir
powers: A set of ten signs each drawn for good fortune in a different undertaking.
description: Lukkustafir, the luck staves of the Huld manuscript, a set of ten separate signs each drawn for good fortune in a different undertaking. The grimoire gives them as a family of practical charms for games, trade, travel, and daily life. They remain among the most reproduced of the Icelandic staves, second only to Vegvísir and Ægishjálmr in modern popularity.

name: The Ljungby Horn
maker: Said to have belonged to a troll
powers: Drinking horn of the troll folk, kept in the church at Ljungby.
description: A horn at the centre of a legend from Ljungby in Småland. A troll who joined a wedding dance was said to have left behind his great drinking horn, which was then kept in the local church; whoever drank from it was cured or grew a beard, according to the variant. The horn is linked in tradition to the troll's magic, and its story is told together with the companion pipe.
source: Småland legend of the Ljungby horn and pipe

name: The Ljungby Pipe
maker: Said to have belonged to a troll
powers: Blowing it was said to set people dancing against their will.
description: The pipe that a troll was said to have left at Ljungby in Småland together with his horn. In the legend the pipe, like the horn, was kept by the parish and remembered as a possession of the troll folk; blowing it was sometimes said to make people dance against their will. The horn and pipe together form one of Sweden's best-known legends of a troll at a human feast.
source: Småland legend of the Ljungby horn and pipe

name: Lund Minster
maker: Romanesque cathedral; legend of the giant Finn
description: Lund Cathedral (Lund domkyrka), the great Romanesque church of the Swedish Middle Ages, begun in the late eleventh century and consecrated in 1145. In legend the giant Finn built the cathedral in exchange for the sun and moon and was turned to stone when he could not win them; a carved giant figure still guards the crypt. The cathedral crowns the story 'Finn the Giant and the Minster of Lund'.
source: Lund Cathedral; Scania legend of the giant Finn

name: The Luckstone
powers: Brings luck and wards off the mare and misfortune.
description: A luckstone (lyckosten), a stone with a natural hole, worn on a cord or kept in the pocket for luck and protection in Swedish folk tradition. Such pierced stones were also called 'hängesten', hanging stones, or 'örngottsstenar' and were hung in stables, on the neck, or by the bed to ward off the mare and misfortune.
source: Swedish folk belief about pierced amulet stones

name: The Lapp Drum
powers: Used for divination and calling the spirit world.
description: The Lapp drum, the sacred drum of the Sami noaidi or shaman, made of a frame of pine with a reindeer-skin head painted with figures in alder-bark juice. The drum was beaten for divination, and the noaidi sought answers in the drumming while its figures of sun, gods, reindeer, and man mirrored the Sami cosmos. Many drums were confiscated by missionaries in the 17th-18th centuries.

name: Lavvu
material: Wood poles with reindeer-hide or canvas covering
description: The conical tent of the Sámi people, raised on a tripod of poles and covered with reindeer hide or, in modern times, canvas. The lavvu is light enough to carry on a sledge or a reindeer and quick to pitch on the open tundra, with the hearth at the center and smoke escaping through the crown. It has been the seasonal home of reindeer-herding families for centuries and is still raised at festivals.

name: The Lur
description: A long S-shaped horn of hammered bronze from the Nordic Bronze Age, cast with an ornamental disc at the mouth. More than fifty lurs survive from Denmark, found in peat bogs and hoards, including the Brudevælte lurs from Zealand. Their curved form and fine engraving make them the oldest preserved brass instruments in the world, likely sounded in cult and sacrifice.

name: Lituus of Romulus
powers: Marked the regions of the sky for augury at Rome's foundation; found unharmed after the burning of the Curia Saliorum.
description: The curved augur's staff with which Romulus marked out the regions of the sky when founding Rome; kept in the Curia Saliorum on the Palatine, it was found unharmed after the temple burned, a portent of Rome's safety. Cicero and Plutarch record the relic, and augurs carried the lituus as the mark of their office.
source: Cicero, De Divinatione; Plutarch, Life of Camillus; Dionysius of Halicarnassus

name: Luzzu
era: Traditional working boat (modern form early 20th century)
maker: Maltese boatwrights, family yards at Marsaxlokk and Gozo
powers: The painted Eye of Osiris on the prow wards off the evil eye and guides the boat home.
description: The luzzu, the brightly painted wooden fishing boat of the Maltese islands, whose prow carries a pair of apotropaic eyes known as the Eye of Osiris or of Horus, an inheritance from Phoenician seafaring meant to ward off the evil eye and guide the boat home; the working fleets of Marsaxlokk still sail with the painted gaze.
source: Ethnographic and maritime documentation of the Maltese fishing tradition

name: Lia Fáil
powers: Cried out beneath the rightful king of Ireland when he stood on it.
description: Lia Fáil, the Stone of Destiny at the hill of Tara, one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann. In tradition it cried out beneath the rightful king of Ireland when he stood on it. The medieval account of the coronation of Conn is the best-known instance of the stone's voice.
source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; Baile in Scáil

name: Lukasa Memory Board
description: The lukasa is a wooden memory board of the Luba of the DRC, its surface studded with beads and pins arranged to encode history, genealogy, and royal protocol. A court historian (mumbudye) 'reads' the board by touch as a mnemonic for sacred knowledge. The arrangement of each board varies with its owner and the legends it preserves.
source: Luba court tradition; scholarly studies (M. Nooter Roberts)

name: Lozi Royal Barge
description: The Lozi royal barge (nalikwanda) is the great wooden vessel that carries the Litunga of the Lozi people of Zambia across the flooded Zambezi at the Kuomboka ceremony. Covered with an immense shroud and propelled by dozens of paddlers, the barge marks the king's seasonal move from lowland to highland palace, a pageant of kingship and river lore.

name: Lei Niho Palaoa (Whale-Tooth Pendant)
description: Pendant of the Hawaiian chiefs made from a carved sperm whale tooth suspended on a braid of human hair, worn by men and women of high rank. The lei niho palaoa was a sign of royalty and genealogical status, and it was forbidden to anyone beneath the chiefly class; the hair cord was itself a gift of honour between the wearer and its giver.
material: sperm whale tooth, braided human hair
maker: Hawaiian craftsmen of the chiefly class

name: Lietuviška Juosta
description: Hand-woven linen and woollen sash, rich with geometric patterns, worn by Lithuanian men and women with festive dress and given as gifts at weddings, christenings and funerals. The symbol system is protective: the sash binds, fastens and marks a sacred boundary, and folk belief made the woven band a mediator, even an offering, between people and mythical beings.
source: Ethnographic studies of Lithuanian sash symbolism (Lietuvių juostų simbolika, Lituanistika)

name: Lielvārde Belt
description: The Lielvārde belt: a wide woven wool sash of red-and-white geometric patterns worn with Latvian folk costume, from central Latvia's Lielvārde region. Legendary as a protective band said to ward off evil, it has since the 1970s been read as a code of the universe and human DNA. Janīna Kursīte traces its red-white symbolism to ancient protective clothing and incantations.
maker: Latvian village weavers of the Lielvārde region
source: Latvijas Kultūras kanons: Lielvārdas josta (2008); folklore researcher Janīna Kursīte

name: Laima's Distaff
description: The distaff of fate in Latvian and Lithuanian belief: a carved spindle-holder on which the goddess Laima, or the forest fairy Lauma, spinning thread, fixes the length and luck of a human life. Folk accounts describe laumas borrowing distaffs and spindles from village women and spinning linen by night. The distaff stands for fate's measuring thread in Latvian spinning dainas.
source: Latvian and Lithuanian folklore accounts of Laima and laumas as spinners of fate (Latvian dainas; Britannica: Laima)
